c.text: A **mass-spring system** vibrates because the spring pulls the mass toward **equilibrium**, while the mass keeps moving. Equilibrium is the resting position toward which the spring pulls.
children: Pull the mass away from equilibrium and release it. The stretched spring pulls it back. The mass is still moving when it reaches equilibrium, so it passes that point and the spring pushes it back from the other side.

c.text: **Longitudinal motion** runs along the spring, so the mass moves left and right. **Transverse motion** runs across the line between the supports, so the mass moves up and down.
children: The drawings show the same repeating pattern in two directions. The transverse springs pull the displaced mass back toward the middle, and its continued motion carries it through the middle.

d.text: A spring pulls a displaced mass toward **equilibrium**, its resting position. The mass has **inertia**, meaning that its motion continues instead of stopping as soon as it reaches that position.
children: If the spring is stretched and the mass is released, the spring pulls the mass back. The mass then passes equilibrium, compresses the spring and is pushed back in the other direction. This repeated motion is **vibration**.

d.text: Returning to equilibrium is different from stopping there. At equilibrium the spring has reached its resting length, but **the mass can still be moving**.
The same vibration can be shown as **longitudinal motion**, left and right along the spring, or **transverse motion**, up and down between the supports.
children: In the transverse drawing, pulling the mass upward stretches the springs. They pull it down toward the middle, and the moving mass continues through the middle. The direction changes, but the explanation of the cycle stays the same.

c.text: **Frequency** is the number of complete back-and-forth cycles in a second. A lower frequency means fewer cycles in the same time.
**Increasing mass lowers frequency** when the spring stays the same. A heavier mass is harder to turn around, so each cycle takes longer.
**Increasing stiffness raises frequency** when the mass stays the same. A stiffer spring pulls back more strongly for the same displacement, so the cycle repeats more quickly.
children: These effects apply to both the longitudinal and transverse drawings. Moving in a different direction does not reverse either rule.

d.text: The number of complete cycles in a second is the **frequency**. This describes **how quickly the motion repeats**, rather than how far the mass moves.
With the spring unchanged, **a heavier mass lowers frequency**. More mass is harder to turn around, so the return trip takes longer.
With the mass unchanged, **a stiffer spring raises frequency**. The stronger restoring pull turns the mass around sooner.
children: Each row changes one property while holding the other fixed. The comparison therefore separates the effect of mass from the effect of stiffness.
Both directions of motion show the same result. Mass and stiffness determine the rate, rather than the orientation of the drawing.

c.text: A **mode** is a particular pattern of vibration of the whole system. The two equal masses and three springs can move in **two modes**.
In **mode 1**, both masses move together. They both rise and fall in the transverse drawing, or both move left and right in the longitudinal drawing.
children: The middle spring moves with them without stretching or compressing. The outer springs provide the restoring pull.

c.text: In **mode 2**, the masses move against each other. When one rises, the other falls. In the longitudinal drawing, they move toward and away from each other.
children: The middle spring now stretches and compresses as well. More stiffness takes part in the motion, so **mode 2 has a higher frequency than mode 1**. The springs themselves have not been replaced or stiffened.

c.text: **Both modes can occur at the same time.** Lifting both masses but making one higher than the other starts a combination of moving together and moving against each other. The combined movement is a mixture of the two modes.

d.text: **Mode 1 and mode 2 are patterns of the whole system, not names for the two masses.** Both masses take part in each pattern.
In **mode 1**, the masses move together, both up and both down, or both left and both right.
children: Their separation stays the same, so the middle spring does not stretch or compress. Only the outer springs provide the changing pull.

d.text: In **mode 2**, the masses move against each other. One moves up while the other moves down, or one moves left while the other moves right.
children: Their changing separation stretches and compresses the middle spring. All three springs now contribute to the restoring action. This greater use of stiffness makes **mode 2 faster than mode 1**, even though the masses and springs are unchanged.

d.text: The bottom row combines **both modes**. Starting both masses above equilibrium, with one higher than the other, produces motion that is partly together and partly against each other.
children: This combined pattern does not add a third mode. It adds the motions of the two available modes.

c.text: A system with **three masses has three modes**. Each mode specifies how all three masses move in relation to one another.
In **mode 1**, all three masses move in the same direction. This is the lowest-frequency pattern because the neighboring masses move mostly together, with relatively little stretching between them.
In **mode 2**, the middle mass stays still while the two outer masses move against each other. One outer mass goes up as the other goes down, or they move left and right in opposite directions.
In **mode 3**, the middle mass moves against both outer masses. The outer masses move together in one direction while the middle mass moves in the other.
children: This creates the most stretching and compression between neighbors, so mode 3 has the highest frequency.

c.text: The three modes can also occur **together**. Their motions add to produce the combined movement in the bottom row.

d.text: **Three masses allow three modes**, each with its own pattern and frequency.
In **mode 1**, all three masses move together. There is relatively little stretching between neighboring masses, so this is the lowest-frequency pattern.
In **mode 2**, the two outer masses move against each other while **the middle mass remains still**.
children: Leaving the middle mass undisturbed and moving the outer masses in opposite directions starts this pattern. A still middle mass remains part of the three-mass system.

d.text: In **mode 3**, the middle mass moves against the two outer masses. When the outer masses rise together, the middle mass falls.
children: Neighboring masses pull against each other more strongly than in the other patterns. There is more stretching and compression, so mode 3 has the highest frequency.

d.text: The bottom row is a **combination of the three modes**, not a fourth mode. Several patterns can contribute to the movement at the same time.

c.text: For these chains, **N masses give N modes**. N means the number of masses. A two-mass chain has two modes, and a six-mass chain has six.
The lowest mode has the masses moving together. Higher modes divide the chain into more regions moving against one another.
children: In the second mode, the left and right parts move in opposite directions. With an odd number of masses, the middle mass stays still.
More motion against neighboring parts creates more stretching and compression, so the higher modes have higher frequencies.

c.text: A **string** has mass and springiness throughout its length. Treating it as many small connected masses and springs explains how it can support the same kinds of vibration patterns.
children: The modes of a chain with separate masses are not generally exact whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.

d.text: For these chains, **N masses give N modes**. N means the number of masses. A two-mass chain has two modes, and a six-mass chain has six.
The lowest mode has the masses moving together. Higher modes divide the chain into more regions moving against one another.
children: In the second mode, the left and right parts move in opposite directions. With an odd number of masses, the middle mass stays still.
More motion against neighboring parts creates more stretching and compression, so the higher modes have higher frequencies.

d.text: A **string** has mass and springiness throughout its length. Treating it as many small connected masses and springs explains how it can support the same kinds of vibration patterns.
children: The modes of a chain with separate masses are not generally exact whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.

c.text: A **fixed–fixed string** cannot move at either end. Its first mode has one moving section. The second has two sections moving against each other, and the third has three.
The mode frequencies are **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of the lowest or **base frequency**. The second mode vibrates twice as fast as the first, and the third vibrates three times as fast.
children: **Hertz**, abbreviated Hz, means cycles per second.

c.text: Several modes can vibrate at once. The combined string adds their motions at each point, producing a more complex shape.
A **spectrum** shows the frequencies present and the strength of each one. A spike marks each active frequency.
children: With five modes present, there are five spikes. With only the third mode present, there is one spike at that mode’s frequency.

d.text: Both ends of a **fixed–fixed string** stay still. The first mode has one moving section, the second has two opposing sections, and higher modes fit more sections into the same length.
The frequencies are **harmonics**, meaning whole-number multiples of the lowest or **base frequency**. The second is twice the first, the third is three times the first, and so on.
children: Frequency is measured in **Hertz**, or cycles per second.

d.text: The combined string adds the motions of its active modes. A complex-looking movement can therefore contain several simple vibration patterns.
In the **spectrum**, a spike’s position tells its **frequency**, and its height tells its **amplitude**, or strength.
children: A taller spike means more of that vibration is present. It does not mean the vibration is faster.
Five active modes produce five spikes. A single active mode produces one spike at its own frequency.

c.text: A **membrane** is a surface that can vibrate. Its moving parts extend in two directions, so its modes divide the surface into regions rather than dividing only a line.
children: The first mode rises and falls as one region. Other modes have neighboring regions moving against one another, with still lines between them.

c.text: Several modes can occur together. Their motions add to make the changing surface shown in the combined panel.
children: The spectrum shows a spike for each active frequency. The equally spaced frequencies in this demonstration are assigned for illustration, rather than calculated as the natural frequencies of this rectangle.

c.text: The **vocal folds** are vibrating tissue with many moving parts. Describing their motion in modes connects that movement with the frequencies present in a voice.

d.text: A **membrane** is a surface that can vibrate. Its moving parts extend in two directions, so its modes divide the surface into regions rather than dividing only a line.
children: The first mode rises and falls as one region. Other modes have neighboring regions moving against one another, with still lines between them.

d.text: Several modes can occur together. Their motions add to make the changing surface shown in the combined panel.
children: The spectrum shows a spike for each active frequency. The equally spaced frequencies in this demonstration are assigned for illustration, rather than calculated as the natural frequencies of this rectangle.

d.text: The **vocal folds** are vibrating tissue with many moving parts. Describing their motion in modes connects that movement with the frequencies present in a voice.

c.text: A **theory** describes how a system works. It can be written in **differential equations**, equations that describe change over time. A **prediction** states what a measurement should show if that account is right.
The prediction for **laryngeal vibration**, the vibration produced by the vocal folds, is a spectrum with evenly spaced peaks called **harmonics**.
children: The spacing is set by the voice’s lowest frequency. Peaks occur at that frequency and its whole-number multiples.

c.text: The test records a voice and examines its spectrum in **Praat**. The measured peaks occur at regular intervals, supporting the prediction.
children: Two voices can have different lowest frequencies and still show the same relationship. Each voice has harmonics spaced by its own base frequency.
Differences in vocal-fold mass help explain different base frequencies. With other properties unchanged, less mass permits faster vibration and a higher base frequency.

d.text: A **theory** explains how a system behaves, while a **prediction** states what should appear in a measurement. **Differential equations** express the changes that the theory describes.

For the vocal folds, the prediction is **evenly spaced harmonics** in the spectrum of laryngeal vibration. The first peak gives the base frequency, and the other peaks occur at its whole-number multiples.
A recording tested in **Praat** shows regularly spaced peaks. The check concerns the **spacing between peaks**, rather than memorizing one person’s frequency.
children: A second voice can have a higher base frequency and wider harmonic spacing. Both voices support the prediction when each has peaks at multiples of its own base frequency.

c.text: A **fixed–free system** has one end that stays still and one end that can move. A **node** is a location that stays still throughout the vibration. An **antinode** is a location with the greatest motion.
children: Each pattern has a node at the fixed end and an antinode at the free end.

c.text: The allowed frequencies are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency, one, three, five and seven times that frequency.
children: The first mode has no still point inside the string. Higher modes add still points and regions moving against one another while keeping the free end moving.

c.text: For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end makes the lowest frequency **half** that of the fixed–fixed string.

d.text: The fixed end of a **fixed–free system** cannot move. It is a **node**. The free end has the largest motion and is an **antinode**.
Every allowed mode must keep those endpoint conditions. Its frequencies follow **one, three, five, seven** times the lowest frequency.
children: **The second mode is the second allowed pattern**, so its frequency is three times the lowest frequency. “Second mode” does not mean twice the frequency.
Each higher pattern adds internal nodes and opposing moving regions while retaining motion at the free end.

d.text: With length and wave speed unchanged, the lowest frequency is **half** that of a string fixed at both ends.

c.text: **Stabilization** means reducing fluctuations and keeping a system near **equilibrium**, a stable balance. The economic example concerns swings in unemployment and inflation.
**Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or **DSGE**, names a theory of how an economy changes and responds to unpredictable events.
children: **Dynamic** refers to change over time. **Stochastic** refers to unpredictable shocks. Stabilization policy aims to make the resulting fluctuations smaller.

d.text: **Stabilization** concerns keeping a system near **equilibrium** and reducing large swings. **Balancing feedback** counters a departure from that balance.
The economic example tracks unemployment and inflation as they change over time. A policy that **damps** a fluctuation makes its swings smaller.
**DSGE** stands for **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**. Dynamic refers to change over time, and stochastic refers to unpredictable events that disturb the system.
children: The theory therefore includes both ongoing change and unexpected shocks, rather than assuming that nothing disturbs the balance.

c.text: The spring pulls a displaced mass toward **equilibrium**, its resting position. The mass keeps moving as it reaches that position, passes it and is pushed back from the other side. The result is **vibration**.
In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves left and right along the spring. In **transverse motion**, it moves up and down between the supports.
children: Both drawings show a restoring pull together with the mass’s continued motion. Changing the drawing’s direction does not change that explanation.

d.text: The spring pulls a displaced mass toward **equilibrium**, its resting position. The mass keeps moving as it reaches that position, passes it and is pushed back from the other side. The result is **vibration**.
In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves left and right along the spring. In **transverse motion**, it moves up and down between the supports.
children: Both drawings show a restoring pull together with the mass’s continued motion. Changing the drawing’s direction does not change that explanation.

c.text: **Frequency** counts complete cycles per second. Adding mass lowers frequency when the spring stays the same, because a heavier mass is harder to turn around.
Adding **stiffness** raises frequency when the mass stays the same. The spring pulls back harder for the same displacement, so the return takes less time.
children: The longitudinal and transverse drawings show the same directions of change. More mass slows the repeating movement, and more stiffness speeds it up.

d.text: **Frequency** counts complete cycles per second. Adding mass lowers frequency when the spring stays the same, because a heavier mass is harder to turn around.
Adding **stiffness** raises frequency when the mass stays the same. The spring pulls back harder for the same displacement, so the return takes less time.
children: The longitudinal and transverse drawings show the same directions of change. More mass slows the repeating movement, and more stiffness speeds it up.

c.text: The two masses have **two modes**, or patterns of vibration. Both masses participate in either mode.
In **mode 1**, the masses move together. The middle spring moves with them without stretching or compressing, so the outer springs supply the restoring pull.
In **mode 2**, the masses move against each other. The middle spring stretches and compresses as well as the outer springs.
children: The extra contribution from the middle spring makes the system effectively stiffer in mode 2. **Mode 2 therefore has a higher frequency**, even though the same masses and springs are present in both modes.

c.text: Lifting both masses to different heights starts **both modes together**. The bottom row combines their motions rather than adding a new mode.

d.text: The two masses have **two modes**, or patterns of vibration. Both masses participate in either mode.
In **mode 1**, the masses move together. The middle spring moves with them without stretching or compressing, so the outer springs supply the restoring pull.
In **mode 2**, the masses move against each other. The middle spring stretches and compresses as well as the outer springs.
children: The extra contribution from the middle spring makes the system effectively stiffer in mode 2. **Mode 2 therefore has a higher frequency**, even though the same masses and springs are present in both modes.

d.text: Lifting both masses to different heights starts **both modes together**. The bottom row combines their motions rather than adding a new mode.

c.text: The three masses have **three modes**. In mode 1, all three move together. In mode 2, the middle mass stays still while the outer masses move against each other. In mode 3, the middle mass moves against both outer masses.
A change in a spring’s **stiffness** matters when that spring stretches or compresses in the pattern being examined.
children: Stiffening a middle spring has little effect on a pattern that hardly stretches it. It raises the frequency of a pattern that does stretch it.

c.text: Making the **middle mass heavier** lowers the frequencies of modes 1 and 3, because the middle mass moves in those modes.
children: Mode 2 stays unchanged because its middle mass does not move. Mode 3 is affected more strongly than mode 1 because the middle mass moves more in that pattern.

d.text: A three-mass system has **three modes**. Mode 1 moves all three masses together. Mode 2 moves the outer masses against each other while the middle stays still. Mode 3 moves the middle against both outer masses.
The effect of **stiffening a spring** depends on how much that spring stretches and compresses in a particular mode.
children: If a spring only moves along with its neighbors, increasing its stiffness contributes little. If its length changes strongly, more stiffness raises that mode’s frequency.

d.text: Increasing the **middle mass** slows modes 1 and 3, where that mass moves. It leaves mode 2 unchanged, where that mass stays still.
children: **The same physical change affects different modes differently.** The mass has not been moved to a new location. Its role changes because the pattern changes.
The middle mass moves more in mode 3 than in mode 1, so the frequency drop is greater in mode 3.

c.text: **N masses give N modes** in these chains. The first mode moves the masses together. The second divides them into two opposing regions, and the third has the middle region moving against the sides.
children: Higher modes involve more stretching between neighboring parts and have higher frequencies.

c.text: A **string** has both mass and springiness along its length. A chain with more and more connected masses and springs approaches that continuous system.
A vibrating string can contain **several modes at once**. Adding those simple patterns produces the complicated movement of the whole string. A **pure tone** contains just one frequency.

d.text: **N masses give N modes** in these chains. The first mode moves the masses together. The second divides them into two opposing regions, and the third has the middle region moving against the sides.
children: Higher modes involve more stretching between neighboring parts and have higher frequencies.

d.text: A **string** has both mass and springiness along its length. A chain with more and more connected masses and springs approaches that continuous system.
A vibrating string can contain **several modes at once**. Adding those simple patterns produces the complicated movement of the whole string. A **pure tone** contains just one frequency.

c.text: The modes of an ideal **fixed–fixed string** have frequencies that are **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of the lowest or **base frequency**.
The first mode contains one moving section. The second fits two opposing sections into the same string length, and the third fits three.
children: Fitting more sections into the same length makes the waves shorter and the frequency higher. The second mode vibrates twice as fast as the first, and the third vibrates three times as fast.

c.text: The combined string adds the motions of several modes. Its **spectrum** separates that combined motion into frequencies.
children: A spike’s position gives its frequency, and its height gives its amplitude. The equal spike heights are a setting of this demonstration.

d.text: The modes of an ideal **fixed–fixed string** have frequencies that are **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of the lowest or **base frequency**.
The first mode contains one moving section. The second fits two opposing sections into the same string length, and the third fits three.
children: Fitting more sections into the same length makes the waves shorter and the frequency higher. The second mode vibrates twice as fast as the first, and the third vibrates three times as fast.

d.text: The combined string adds the motions of several modes. Its **spectrum** separates that combined motion into frequencies.
children: A spike’s position gives its frequency, and its height gives its amplitude. The equal spike heights are a setting of this demonstration.

c.text: **Increasing mass lowers frequency; increasing stiffness raises it.** The symbols **m** and **k** stand for mass and stiffness. The effect depends on what the changed part does in a particular mode.
Added mass matters most **where there is strong motion**. Adding it at a node, a location that stays still, leaves that mode’s frequency unchanged.
Added stiffness matters **where there is stretching or compression**. Neighboring parts can stretch against one another around a still point even though the point itself does not move.
children: A region can move strongly with little change in spacing between neighboring parts. Strong motion therefore does not mean strong stretching.

c.text: The endpoints determine the allowed frequency pattern. A **fixed–fixed string** has whole-number harmonics. A **fixed–free system** has odd multiples of its lowest frequency.

d.text: The symbols **m** and **k** mean mass and stiffness. **More mass lowers frequency, while more stiffness raises it.** The downward arrow printed beside stiffness in the first line is a typo, corrected by the stiffness principle below it.

For added mass, ask whether the changed part **moves in that mode**. More movement means a greater frequency drop. At a node, where that part stays still throughout the cycle, added mass has no effect.
For added stiffness, follow the **stretching or compression between neighboring parts**. A still point can sit between parts that strongly stretch against one another.
children: A node is not simply a point caught at equilibrium for one instant. It remains still through the cycle. This is why a snapshot alone cannot identify every node.

d.text: A chain with **N masses has N modes**. Fixed–fixed string modes have whole-number harmonic frequencies, while fixed–free modes have odd-multiple frequencies.

c.text: In the first mode of this fixed–fixed string, the **middle moves most**, while the ends stay still. The middle region moves up and down with little stretching between nearby parts.
Near a fixed end there is little movement, but neighboring parts stretch against one another. **Strong motion and strong stretching occur in different regions.**
children: Higher modes repeat this alternation at more places along the string. A local change must therefore be matched to the pattern of the mode being examined.

d.text: In the first mode of this fixed–fixed string, the **middle moves most**, while the ends stay still. The middle region moves up and down with little stretching between nearby parts.
Near a fixed end there is little movement, but neighboring parts stretch against one another. **Strong motion and strong stretching occur in different regions.**
children: Higher modes repeat this alternation at more places along the string. A local change must therefore be matched to the pattern of the mode being examined.

c.text: The marked section has **strong motion in mode 4** and **strong stretching around a still point in mode 5**. Making that one section heavier and stiffer therefore affects the two modes differently.
In **mode 4**, added mass lowers the frequency because the section moves. Added stiffness has little effect because there is little stretching at that location.
In **mode 5**, added mass has no effect because the marked point stays still. Added stiffness raises the frequency because neighboring parts stretch and compress there.
The combined result is **mode 4 down and mode 5 up**. Predicting the effect of a small local change is called **perturbation**.

d.text: Both changes are made at **the same marked location**. Mode 4 moves strongly there. Mode 5 has a still point there, with strong stretching around it.
For **mode 4**, adding mass slows the moving section and lowers frequency. Stiffening that section has little effect because it does little stretching.
For **mode 5**, adding mass to a point that stays still does not slow the mode. Increasing stiffness does matter because neighboring parts stretch against one another there, so frequency rises.
**Making one section heavier and stiffer lowers mode 4 and raises mode 5.** The opposite results come from how each mode uses the location.
children: This reasoning is **perturbation**, predicting what a small change does to the system. Adding mass to a moving region of a drum lowers a frequency, while adding it at a still point leaves that mode unchanged.

c.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface. Its first mode moves as one region, while higher modes have more regions moving against one another.
children: The two-number labels identify how the surface is divided in its two directions. A pattern with two regions in one direction has those regions moving oppositely.

c.text: Several membrane modes can occur **at the same time**. Their motions add to make the combined surface, and the spectrum has a spike for each active frequency.
children: The equally spaced frequencies and equal spike heights are assigned for this illustration. They are not a calculation of this rectangle’s natural frequencies.

c.text: The **vocal folds** contain many connected moving parts, so their vibration can also be described through modes.

d.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface. Its first mode moves as one region, while higher modes have more regions moving against one another.
children: The two-number labels identify how the surface is divided in its two directions. A pattern with two regions in one direction has those regions moving oppositely.

d.text: Several membrane modes can occur **at the same time**. Their motions add to make the combined surface, and the spectrum has a spike for each active frequency.
children: The equally spaced frequencies and equal spike heights are assigned for this illustration. They are not a calculation of this rectangle’s natural frequencies.

d.text: The **vocal folds** contain many connected moving parts, so their vibration can also be described through modes.

c.text: A **prediction** states what a measurement should show. For a voice, the prediction is a spectrum with **harmonics** at regular intervals, starting from that voice’s base frequency.
A spectral slice in **Praat** tests this by showing peaks at the base frequency and approximately twice and three times that frequency.
children: Different voices have different base frequencies. The predicted relationship is regular spacing within each voice, rather than one shared frequency for everyone.

c.text: Changing **mass or stiffness in the vocal folds** can change the vibration. A **nodule** adds mass locally, and different modes can be affected by different amounts.

d.text: The predicted **harmonics** are evenly spaced peaks in the spectrum of vocal-fold vibration. A spectral slice in **Praat** tests whether the peaks occur at multiples of the base frequency.
The measured second and third peaks are about twice and three times the first. A different voice can have a different starting frequency and still show the same pattern.
Changing the **mass or stiffness of part of the vocal folds** can change how they vibrate. A nodule adds mass locally, and its effect depends on which parts move in the different modes.
children: This application concerns a change in the vibrating tissue, rather than a change in the air resonances used to shape vowels.

c.text: In a **fixed–free system**, the fixed end is a **node**, a location with no motion, and the free end is an **antinode**, a location with the greatest motion.

The frequencies are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency. The first mode contains one section from no motion to maximum motion. The second contains three such sections, and the third contains five.
children: The endpoint conditions must stay the same in every mode. This is why the allowed patterns skip the even multiples.

c.text: The idealized **vocal tract** is closed at the vocal-fold end and open at the lips. Its air has little back-and-forth motion at the closed end and can move freely at the open end.

d.text: **Fixed and free describe motion at the ends of the model.** A node stays still, while an antinode has maximum motion. Every fixed–free mode must retain a node at one end and an antinode at the other.
The allowed frequencies follow **one, three, five** times the lowest frequency. The second allowed mode therefore has three times the first mode’s frequency.
children: For the same length and wave speed, the lowest frequency is half that of a string fixed at both ends.

d.text: In the idealized **vocal tract**, the vocal-fold end is closed to the air’s back-and-forth motion, while the open lips permit that motion.
children: The air can vibrate in several modes at once. Its fixed–free endpoint conditions apply to every one of those modes.

c.text: The air in the **vocal tract** has mass and springiness. Its **inertia** resists changes in motion, and its springiness supplies a restoring effect when it is compressed.
children: The model is fixed at the **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds, and free at the lips. The air moves back and forth along the tube.

c.text: **F1** and **F2** are the first and second **formants**, the resonances of the air in the vocal tract. A resonance is a frequency at which that air vibrates strongly. F1 is the lowest-frequency mode, and F2 is the next one.
children: In this uniform fixed–free tube, F2 is three times F1. The marked locations identify the modeled constrictions for /a/, /i/ and /u/.

d.text: The air in the **vocal tract** both moves and compresses. Its mass contributes **inertia**, while compression and expansion reveal its **springiness**.
children: The chain is fixed at the **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds, and free at the lips. These labels describe whether air can move back and forth at each end.

d.text: A **formant** is a resonance of the air in the vocal tract, a frequency at which that air vibrates strongly. **F1** names the lowest resonance, and **F2** names the second.
children: In the uniform fixed–free tube, F2 is three times F1. The number 2 orders the formants. It does not mean twice F1.
The marks at one third and two thirds of the tract length are measured from the glottis. The free end is the lip location.

c.text: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the vocal tract. Vowels differ in where the tongue or lips create that narrowing.
children: **High** and **low** describe tongue height. **Front**, **central** and **back** describe its position from front to back.

c.text: The high front vowel in **Dean** has a constriction near two thirds of the distance from the glottis. **Dune** has rounding at the lips. **Don** has a constriction near one third of the distance from the glottis.
children: **Done** is the central example with no marked constriction. **Dan** is shown as low and front.

c.text: The constriction’s **location** matters because the air does different amounts of moving and compressing at different places in each mode.

d.text: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the vocal tract. Vowels differ in where the tongue or lips create that narrowing.
children: **High** and **low** describe tongue height. **Front**, **central** and **back** describe its position from front to back.

d.text: The high front vowel in **Dean** has a constriction near two thirds of the distance from the glottis. **Dune** has rounding at the lips. **Don** has a constriction near one third of the distance from the glottis.
children: **Done** is the central example with no marked constriction. **Dan** is shown as low and front.

d.text: The constriction’s **location** matters because the air does different amounts of moving and compressing at different places in each mode.

c.text: The same location can behave differently in **mode 1 and mode 2**. Near the lips, both modes have strong motion. Farther inside the tract, one mode can have strong motion where another has strong compression.
**F1 and F2 are air resonances**, not the harmonics of the vocal folds. A constriction changes a formant according to what the air does at that location in its mode.
children: The /a/ mark is near one third of the distance from the glottis. The /i/ mark is near two thirds, and /u/ marks the lip end.

d.text: The same location can behave differently in **mode 1 and mode 2**. Near the lips, both modes have strong motion. Farther inside the tract, one mode can have strong motion where another has strong compression.
**F1 and F2 are air resonances**, not the harmonics of the vocal folds. A constriction changes a formant according to what the air does at that location in its mode.
children: The /a/ mark is near one third of the distance from the glottis. The /i/ mark is near two thirds, and /u/ marks the lip end.

c.text: For **/u/**, lip rounding narrows the air passage at the **free end**. This increases the effective mass of the air in a region where both modes move strongly.
More mass at a moving location slows a mode. **Both F1 and F2 therefore decrease.** There is little compression at the lip end, so the added stiffness contributes little to the change.

d.text: Lip rounding for **/u/** increases the effective mass of air near the lips. This is **loading the free end**.
Both mode 1 and mode 2 have **strong motion and little compression** there. The extra mass slows both modes, while the extra stiffness has little effect.
children: **F1 goes down and F2 goes down.** The location’s behavior explains why both formants move in the same direction.

c.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is near **two thirds of the distance from the glottis**. It increases mass and stiffness at the same location, but the two modes use that location differently.
Mode 1 has strong motion there. Added mass slows that vibration, so **F1 decreases**.
children: Mode 2 has strong compression and expansion there. Added stiffness strengthens the restoring action, so **F2 increases**.

d.text: The constriction for **/i/** lies near two thirds of the distance from the glottis. Narrowing the tract there increases both effective mass and stiffness.
In **mode 1**, the air mostly moves back and forth. More moving mass slows the cycle, so **F1 goes down**.
In **mode 2**, the air mostly compresses and expands. More stiffness makes the restoring action stronger, so **F2 goes up**.
children: The two effects do not cancel because motion matters more in one mode and compression matters more in the other.

c.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is near **one third of the distance from the glottis**. In mode 1, compression and expansion are strong there, so added stiffness raises **F1**.
In mode 2, motion is strong at that location, so added mass lowers **F2**.
children: The result is **F1 up and F2 down**. One narrowing has opposite effects on the two resonances because each mode has a different pattern.

d.text: The /a/ constriction is near **one third of the distance from the glottis**. It makes that part of the air heavier and stiffer.
Mode 1 has strong compression there, so the stiffness increase raises **F1**. Mode 2 has strong motion there, so the mass increase lowers **F2**.
children: **F1 goes up and F2 goes down.** The prediction follows the local motion and compression in each mode, rather than a rule that every constriction raises or lowers every formant.

c.text: A local change affects a mode according to **what changes and what that location does**. Added mass lowers frequency when the part moves. Added stiffness raises frequency when neighboring parts stretch or compress.
The symbols **m** and **k** stand for mass and stiffness. Raising both at one location does not guarantee cancellation, because their influence depends on the mode.
children: At a still point, more mass has little effect but more stiffness can matter strongly. At a strongly moving location with little stretching, more mass matters most.

d.text: A local change affects a mode according to **what changes and what that location does**. Added mass lowers frequency when the part moves. Added stiffness raises frequency when neighboring parts stretch or compress.
The symbols **m** and **k** stand for mass and stiffness. Raising both at one location does not guarantee cancellation, because their influence depends on the mode.
children: At a still point, more mass has little effect but more stiffness can matter strongly. At a strongly moving location with little stretching, more mass matters most.

c.text: **Motion** is the back-and-forth travel of a part of the air. **Compression** is the change in spacing between neighboring parts. These are different properties.
children: Lines of air that move together can travel a long way without becoming closer together. Compression occurs when their spacing changes.

c.text: In the first mode, air has little motion near the closed glottal end, where compression is strong. Near the open lips, motion is strongest and compression is weakest.
Higher modes contain more alternating regions of strong motion and strong compression. This lets one constriction affect two formants differently.

d.text: Follow both **how far a line of air moves** and **how its distance from neighboring lines changes**. The first is motion, and the second reveals compression and expansion.
At the open lips, neighboring lines move back and forth together with little change in their spacing. This region has strong motion but little compression.
Near the closed end, the air cannot move far, but neighboring lines repeatedly crowd together and spread apart. This region has strong compression.
children: A line that stays still can have neighboring air moving toward and away from it. Stillness at a point therefore does not remove springiness around it.

d.text: The higher modes fit more alternating motion and compression regions into the same tract. The effect of a constriction must be checked separately for each formant.

c.text: **More mass lowers frequency; more stiffness raises it.** The symbols **m** and **k** stand for mass and stiffness. Raising both does not automatically make their effects cancel.
The outcome depends on **location within a mode**. At a still point with strong stretching around it, added mass contributes little while added stiffness raises the frequency.
children: At a strongly moving location with little stretching, added mass lowers frequency while added stiffness contributes little.

c.text: The same system has several modes, and each uses its parts differently. A prediction must therefore refer to a **particular mode**, rather than to “the frequency” without specifying which one.

d.text: Raising **mass** tends to lower frequency, and raising **stiffness** tends to raise it. Those opposite tendencies do not establish that the effects are equal.
Cancellation requires the effective changes to **balance**. In a system with many parts, the mode’s motion and stretching at the changed location determine how strongly each effect counts.

Where a point stays still but nearby parts stretch strongly, added mass has no effect while added stiffness raises frequency. Where motion is strong and stretching is weak, added mass lowers frequency while added stiffness contributes little.
children: The change can therefore raise one mode’s frequency and lower another’s even when the same part becomes both heavier and stiffer.

c.text: These chains have equal masses and springs, with both ends fixed. **N masses give N modes**, so each row has as many possible patterns as it has masses.
The lowest mode moves the masses together. Higher modes divide the chain into more regions moving against one another.
children: More relative movement between neighbors means more stretching and compression, which makes the higher-frequency patterns faster.

c.text: A chain with separate masses does not generally have frequencies that are exact whole-number multiples. The **ideal string** is the continuous system with that harmonic relationship.

d.text: These chains have equal masses and springs, with both ends fixed. **N masses give N modes**, so each row has as many possible patterns as it has masses.
The lowest mode moves the masses together. Higher modes divide the chain into more regions moving against one another.
children: More relative movement between neighbors means more stretching and compression, which makes the higher-frequency patterns faster.

d.text: A chain with separate masses does not generally have frequencies that are exact whole-number multiples. The **ideal string** is the continuous system with that harmonic relationship.

c.text: A string fixed at both ends must have **no motion at each end**. The first mode contains one **half-wave packet**, a section that runs from a still point through a moving region to another still point.
The second mode fits two half-wave packets into the same length, and the fifth fits five. More packets mean shorter waves and higher frequencies.
children: The second harmonic vibrates at twice the **base frequency**, and the fifth at five times that frequency. These whole-number multiples are **harmonics**.

c.text: The model of **vocal-fold vibration** predicts harmonics as well. A voice’s base frequency can differ from another’s while the whole-number relationship remains.

d.text: A string fixed at both ends must have **no motion at each end**. The first mode contains one **half-wave packet**, a section that runs from a still point through a moving region to another still point.
The second mode fits two half-wave packets into the same length, and the fifth fits five. More packets mean shorter waves and higher frequencies.
children: The second harmonic vibrates at twice the **base frequency**, and the fifth at five times that frequency. These whole-number multiples are **harmonics**.

d.text: The model of **vocal-fold vibration** predicts harmonics as well. A voice’s base frequency can differ from another’s while the whole-number relationship remains.

c.text: A string can vibrate in **several modes at once**. Adding the movement from each mode at every point gives the changing shape of the combined string.
The higher modes repeat more quickly. While the first completes one cycle, the fifth completes five in this harmonic system.
children: The spectrum has one spike for each active frequency. Its equal spike heights are deliberately set for this demonstration, rather than being a requirement for every string sound.

d.text: A string can vibrate in **several modes at once**. Adding the movement from each mode at every point gives the changing shape of the combined string.
The higher modes repeat more quickly. While the first completes one cycle, the fifth completes five in this harmonic system.
children: The spectrum has one spike for each active frequency. Its equal spike heights are deliberately set for this demonstration, rather than being a requirement for every string sound.

c.text: A **membrane** extends in two directions. Its mode labels use two numbers to describe the moving regions in those directions.
children: In **(1, 1)**, the surface rises and falls as one region. In **(2, 1)** or **(1, 2)**, two regions move against each other. In **(2, 2)**, four regions alternate, and in **(3, 1)** there are three regions along one direction.

c.text: The combined surface adds these separate motions. Its spectrum shows the active frequencies at the marked pickup point.
children: The harmonic frequencies in this illustration are assigned teaching values. They are not the natural frequencies calculated for the pictured rectangle.

d.text: A **membrane** extends in two directions. Its mode labels use two numbers to describe the moving regions in those directions.
children: In **(1, 1)**, the surface rises and falls as one region. In **(2, 1)** or **(1, 2)**, two regions move against each other. In **(2, 2)**, four regions alternate, and in **(3, 1)** there are three regions along one direction.

d.text: The combined surface adds these separate motions. Its spectrum shows the active frequencies at the marked pickup point.
children: The harmonic frequencies in this illustration are assigned teaching values. They are not the natural frequencies calculated for the pictured rectangle.

c.text: A **fixed–free system** has a **node** at its fixed end and an **antinode** at its free end. A node stays still through the cycle, while an antinode has the greatest motion.
Its first mode runs from no motion at one end to maximum motion at the other. Higher patterns must keep both endpoint conditions.
children: The allowed frequencies are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency, one, three, five and seven times that frequency.

c.text: For the same length and wave speed, this system has a lowest frequency **half** that of a string fixed at both ends. The idealized air in the vocal tract has fixed–free endpoint conditions.

d.text: A **fixed–free system** has a **node** at its fixed end and an **antinode** at its free end. A node stays still through the cycle, while an antinode has the greatest motion.
Its first mode runs from no motion at one end to maximum motion at the other. Higher patterns must keep both endpoint conditions.
children: The allowed frequencies are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency, one, three, five and seven times that frequency.

d.text: For the same length and wave speed, this system has a lowest frequency **half** that of a string fixed at both ends. The idealized air in the vocal tract has fixed–free endpoint conditions.

c.text: A **quarter-wave packet** runs from a node, where there is no motion, to an antinode, where motion is greatest. A fixed–free pattern must begin and end in this way.
The allowed modes contain **one, three, five or seven quarter-wave packets**. Adding a pair of packets keeps an antinode at the free end.
children: An even number would put a node at that free end, so it would fail the endpoint condition.

c.text: More packets within the same length mean shorter waves and a higher frequency. The odd packet counts explain the **odd-multiple frequency pattern**.

d.text: The fixed end is a **node** and the free end is an **antinode**. A **quarter-wave packet** is the part of the spatial pattern between those two kinds of location.
The first mode fits one packet. The second fits three, the third fits five, and the fourth fits seven.
children: Packets are counted along the length of the system. They are pieces of the pattern, rather than separate masses or separate times in the motion.

d.text: The count must stay **odd** to finish at a moving free end. Adding two packets preserves that condition, while an even count would finish at a still node.
children: Fitting more packets into the same length makes the waves shorter and their frequency higher.

c.text: Count the **quarter-wave packets** from the fixed bottom to the free top. The first mode contains one packet, the second three, the third five and the fourth seven.
Each pattern must start at a **node** and end at an **antinode**. The extra packets add still points inside while preserving motion at the free end.
children: The mode number counts allowed patterns. It does not give the multiple of the lowest frequency. The second mode has three times that frequency.

d.text: Count the **quarter-wave packets** from the fixed bottom to the free top. The first mode contains one packet, the second three, the third five and the fourth seven.
Each pattern must start at a **node** and end at an **antinode**. The extra packets add still points inside while preserving motion at the free end.
children: The mode number counts allowed patterns. It does not give the multiple of the lowest frequency. The second mode has three times that frequency.

c.text: The **vocal tract** contains air that has both mass and springiness. The chain models the air’s **inertia**, its resistance to changes in motion, and its restoring response when compressed.
The model is fixed at the vocal-fold end and free at the lips. Its lowest mode is the **first formant, F1**, and the next is the **second formant, F2**.
children: In a uniform fixed–free tube, the frequencies follow one, three and five times F1. F2 therefore has three times F1’s frequency.

c.text: The marked /a/, /i/ and /u/ locations identify where the modeled constrictions act. Their effect depends on how each mode moves or compresses there.

d.text: The air’s **mass** allows continued motion, while its **springiness** produces a restoring effect when air is squeezed. The mass-spring chain makes those two properties visible.
The fixed end represents the vocal-fold end of the tract, and the free end represents the lips. **F1** and **F2** name the first and second air resonances, or **formants**.
In this **uniform fixed–free tube**, F2 is three times F1 and F3 is five times F1.
children: The number in F2 orders the resonances from lowest to highest. It does not mean twice F1. The odd-multiple relationship describes the uniform tube, rather than every vowel shape.

d.text: The three marked positions locate the /a/, /i/ and /u/ constrictions. Each position can have a different role in mode 1 and mode 2.

c.text: In the idealized tube, the **vocal-fold end is closed** and the **lip end is open**. Air has little back-and-forth motion at the closed end and its greatest motion near the open end.

The lines represent groups of air molecules. **Changing spacing** between neighboring lines indicates compression and expansion. Lines that travel together without changing spacing show strong motion with little compression.
Mode 1 has no internal motion node. Mode 2 adds one, and mode 3 adds two. Around a node, neighboring air can repeatedly compress and expand even though the node itself stays still.
The resonances are the **formants**, F1, F2 and F3. The uniform fixed–free model has odd-multiple frequencies. Changing the shape of the tract changes those resonances.

d.text: The **closed vocal-fold end** prevents back-and-forth air motion, while the **open lip end** allows it. These are the fixed and free ends of the model.
**Motion and compression are different.** A line can move far while keeping the same distance from its neighbors. Compression happens when those distances shrink, and expansion when they grow.
A **node** stays still, but the air beside it can move toward and away from it. Strong compression around a still point is therefore consistent with no motion at that point.
children: Mode 1 has its only motion node at the closed end. Mode 2 adds one internal node, and mode 3 adds two.

d.text: **F1, F2 and F3** order the air resonances from lowest to highest. Their odd-multiple relationship belongs to the uniform fixed–free model. A constriction changes the tract’s resonances.

c.text: Vowels differ in where the tongue and lips create a **constriction**, a narrowing in the vocal tract. **High/low** describes tongue height, and **front/back** describes its location along the tract.

The high front vowel in **Dean** has a narrowing near two thirds of the distance from the **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds. The low back vowel in **Don** has a narrowing near one third.
children: **Dune** includes lip rounding and a back tongue constriction. **Done** is the central, unmarked-constriction example, while **Dan** is low and front.

c.text: The location matters because different parts of each mode have different amounts of motion and compression. The modeled lip constriction of **/u/** has a strong effect on the first two formants.

For **/u/**, the back tongue constriction and the lip constriction play different roles. In this account, the back constriction is the example where the effects balance and leave the formants unchanged. The lip constriction lowers the first two formants.

d.text: Vowels differ in where the tongue and lips create a **constriction**, a narrowing in the vocal tract. **High/low** describes tongue height, and **front/back** describes its location along the tract.

The high front vowel in **Dean** has a narrowing near two thirds of the distance from the **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds. The low back vowel in **Don** has a narrowing near one third.
children: **Dune** includes lip rounding and a back tongue constriction. **Done** is the central, unmarked-constriction example, while **Dan** is low and front.

d.text: The location matters because different parts of each mode have different amounts of motion and compression. The modeled lip constriction of **/u/** has a strong effect on the first two formants.

For **/u/**, the back tongue constriction and the lip constriction play different roles. In this account, the back constriction is the example where the effects balance and leave the formants unchanged. The lip constriction lowers the first two formants.

c.text: A **constriction** narrows the air passage and raises both its effective **mass** and **stiffness**. These changes tend to affect frequency in opposite directions.
Their effects do not automatically cancel. The result depends on **what the air is doing at the constriction in a particular mode**.
children: At a region with strong motion, added mass matters most and tends to lower that formant.
At a region with strong compression, added stiffness matters most and tends to raise that formant.

c.text: The same constriction can therefore lower one formant and raise another. Each mode uses the location differently.

d.text: Narrowing the tract increases both effective **mass** and **stiffness** of the air at the constriction. More mass tends to slow vibration, while more stiffness tends to speed it up.

A location’s **motion and compression** decide which effect is stronger. Where air mostly travels back and forth, the mass increase matters most. Where it mostly compresses and expands, the stiffness increase matters most.
children: The increases act at one location, but that location can be strongly moving in one mode and strongly compressing in another.

d.text: This is why **one constriction can shift two formants in opposite directions**. Raising both properties is not enough information to predict cancellation.

c.text: At each location in the air column, distinguish **movement of the air** from **change in spacing between neighboring parts**. The second is compression and expansion.
A constriction at a strongly moving location tends to **lower that mode’s formant** because of added mass. A constriction where compression is strong tends to **raise it** because of added stiffness.
children: Near the closed end, motion is weak and compression is strong. Near the open lips, motion is strong and compression is weak.

d.text: At each location in the air column, distinguish **movement of the air** from **change in spacing between neighboring parts**. The second is compression and expansion.
A constriction at a strongly moving location tends to **lower that mode’s formant** because of added mass. A constriction where compression is strong tends to **raise it** because of added stiffness.
children: Near the closed end, motion is weak and compression is strong. Near the open lips, motion is strong and compression is weak.

c.text: Both modes move strongly at the **lip end**. Inside the tube their patterns differ, so the same marked point can have strong motion in one mode and strong compression in the other.
The modeled **/a/** constriction is near one third of the distance from the glottis, and **/i/** is near two thirds. **/u/** loads the lip end.
children: For each formant, the local movement decides how much added mass matters, and local compression decides how much added stiffness matters.

d.text: Both modes move strongly at the **lip end**. Inside the tube their patterns differ, so the same marked point can have strong motion in one mode and strong compression in the other.
The modeled **/a/** constriction is near one third of the distance from the glottis, and **/i/** is near two thirds. **/u/** loads the lip end.
children: For each formant, the local movement decides how much added mass matters, and local compression decides how much added stiffness matters.

c.text: For **/u/**, lip rounding narrows the passage at the free end. The effective mass and stiffness of the air increase there.
Both modes have **strong motion and little compression at the lips**. The added mass therefore slows both modes, while the added stiffness has little effect.
children: The prediction is **F1 down and F2 down**. A recording that moves from schwa into /u/ shows both formants dropping.

d.text: **Loading the free end** means increasing effective mass near the lips. Lip rounding for **/u/** produces that change in the model.
The air moves strongly there in **both mode 1 and mode 2**. Its neighboring parts have little relative compression, so added mass matters much more than added stiffness.
Both modes slow, giving **lower F1 and lower F2**. The recorded change from schwa into /u/ shows the same downward movement of both formants.

c.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is near **two thirds of the distance from the glottis**. The same narrowing raises both effective mass and stiffness there.
Mode 1 has strong motion at that location, so the added mass lowers **F1**. Mode 2 has strong compression and expansion there, so the added stiffness raises **F2**.
children: The recording from schwa into /i/ shows the predicted result, **F1 down and F2 up**.

d.text: The **/i/** constriction is near two thirds of the distance from the glottis. Its effect depends on the pattern of each mode, not simply on narrowing the passage.
In **mode 1**, that region mostly moves. Increasing its mass slows the mode, so **F1 decreases**.
In **mode 2**, that region mostly compresses and expands. Increasing its stiffness strengthens the restoring action, so **F2 increases**.
children: A recording that changes from schwa into /i/ shows the same separation, with F1 falling and F2 rising.

c.text: The modeled **/a/** constriction is near **one third of the distance from the glottis**. Compression is strong there in mode 1, so added stiffness raises **F1**.
Motion is strong there in mode 2, so added mass lowers **F2**.
children: The result is **F1 up and F2 down**. The two formants respond differently because the same location participates differently in their modes.

d.text: For **/a/**, the narrowing is near one third of the distance from the glottis. It adds effective mass and stiffness at that location.
The first mode has strong compression there, so increased stiffness raises **F1**. The second mode has strong motion there, so increased mass lowers **F2**.
children: The outcome, **F1 up and F2 down**, follows the motion and compression at the marked location. A narrowing does not push every resonance in the same direction.

c.text: **Motion and compression alternate along the air column.** In one region, air travels strongly with little change in spacing. In another, the spacing changes strongly while local motion is small.
Higher modes place those regions differently. A constriction can therefore fall in a moving region for one formant and a compressing region for another.
children: Predict the effect separately for each mode. Added moving mass lowers its frequency, while added stiffness where air compresses raises it.

d.text: **Motion and compression alternate along the air column.** In one region, air travels strongly with little change in spacing. In another, the spacing changes strongly while local motion is small.
Higher modes place those regions differently. A constriction can therefore fall in a moving region for one formant and a compressing region for another.
children: Predict the effect separately for each mode. Added moving mass lowers its frequency, while added stiffness where air compresses raises it.

c.text: In **source-filter theory**, the **source** is vocal-fold vibration and the **filter** is the air in the vocal tract. They contribute different patterns to the same vowel sound.
The source supplies **harmonics**, the evenly spaced peaks at multiples of its base frequency. The tract’s **formants** determine which harmonics come through strongly.
children: Harmonics near a formant have greater amplitude, while those between formants have less amplitude.

c.text: The **envelope** is the broad outline traced by the harmonic heights. Changing the vowel moves the formants and changes this outline.
children: With the source held fixed, the harmonic frequencies stay in place. Their **heights change** because the filter has changed.

d.text: A vowel combines **source** and **filter**. Vocal-fold vibration supplies the source harmonics. Air resonances in the vocal tract supply the filter formants.
The filter changes **how strongly each harmonic appears**. Harmonics near a formant become tall peaks, while those between formants remain shorter.
children: A formant is therefore visible through a group of harmonic heights. It is not simply another harmonic added between them.

d.text: The **envelope** is the smooth overall outline of those heights. A different vowel has different formant positions and a different envelope.
children: When the source stays the same, changing the vowel leaves the harmonics at the same frequencies and changes their amplitudes.

c.text: The **/i/** filter has a **low F1** and a **high F2**. Harmonics near those resonances become strong, leaving a wide gap between the two groups of tall peaks.
The source’s harmonic frequencies stay the same. What changes is their **amplitude**, giving the envelope its /i/ pattern.
children: The widely separated formants agree with the modeled /i/ constriction, which lowers F1 and raises F2.

d.text: The **/i/** filter has a **low F1** and a **high F2**. Harmonics near those resonances become strong, leaving a wide gap between the two groups of tall peaks.
The source’s harmonic frequencies stay the same. What changes is their **amplitude**, giving the envelope its /i/ pattern.
children: The widely separated formants agree with the modeled /i/ constriction, which lowers F1 and raises F2.

c.text: The **/a/** filter has a **higher F1** and a **lower F2**, placing the first two formants closer together. Harmonics near them become tall and form a broad low-frequency group.
The harmonics remain at the frequencies supplied by the source. The filter changes their **heights**, creating the envelope for /a/.
children: The formant positions agree with the modeled constriction that raises F1 and lowers F2.

d.text: The **/a/** filter has a **higher F1** and a **lower F2**, placing the first two formants closer together. Harmonics near them become tall and form a broad low-frequency group.
The harmonics remain at the frequencies supplied by the source. The filter changes their **heights**, creating the envelope for /a/.
children: The formant positions agree with the modeled constriction that raises F1 and lowers F2.

c.text: A **spectrum** displays the frequencies and amplitudes in one short portion of sound. A **spectrogram** places successive spectra in time so that changing speech sounds can be followed.
In the spectrogram, **time runs left to right**, **frequency runs bottom to top**, and **darkness shows amplitude**. Darker regions contain stronger energy.
children: A formant appears as a dark band because harmonics near that air resonance have high amplitude.

c.text: During **/i/**, F1 is low and F2 is high, so the bands are far apart. Moving into **/a/** raises the low band and lowers the high band, bringing the formants closer together.

d.text: A **spectrogram** follows sound through time. It combines many short spectra, rather than showing only one moment.
Read **time horizontally** and **frequency vertically**. **Amplitude becomes darkness**, so a tall peak in a spectrum becomes a dark region at its frequency.
A **formant band** marks a region of strong harmonic energy around an air resonance. Following the band tracks how that resonance changes as the tract changes shape.
children: The /i/ portion has low F1 and high F2. In the /a/ portion the first band rises and the second falls, so they become closer together.

c.text: **Harmonics reveal formants through their amplitudes.** Closely spaced harmonics give many peaks around each formant, making its overall shape easier to identify.
A higher **F0**, the base frequency of vocal-fold vibration, spreads the harmonics farther apart. Fewer peaks then fall near each formant, and a formant can lie between them.
children: Changing F0 does not by itself move the filter’s formants. It changes how densely the harmonics show their shape.

c.text: This makes formants harder to identify in high-pitched voices, including those of toddlers and sopranos. A widely spaced harmonic can be mistaken for the formant region that strengthens it.

d.text: A **formant** is an air resonance, while a **harmonic** is a multiple of the vocal-fold base frequency. A formant strengthens nearby harmonics, so their heights reveal its position.
With low **F0**, many closely spaced harmonics trace each formant region. Raising F0 spreads the harmonics apart and leaves fewer peaks to show the same filter.
children: A formant can fall between widely spaced harmonics. The difficulty is then seeing the resonance from a few peaks, rather than the formant disappearing.

d.text: High-pitched voices can therefore make formants hard to locate. The harmonic spacing changes with F0 even if the **vocal-tract filter stays fixed**.

review.sourceText: Source text, existing Original C/D, source-page order and original visual assets were compared. Static contact sheets cover every source page. For all 15 distinct embedded videos, frames at 12%, 47% and 79% were inspected to review the diagrams and visible changes. This is a sampled visual check, not a claim of complete animation/audio playback.
review.styleReference: PSYC301 Version20 Working Memory complete-sentence main bullets and explanatory sub-bullets; no inherited count/length quotas.
review.omissions: Friction details, decorative discussion, source analogies, repetitive instructions to understand rather than memorize, and routine equation/numerical recitals were removed from these new copies. Scientific terms and conceptual relationships remain.
review.corrections: The three-mass lowest mode is described as little relative stretching rather than none, consistent with the shown unequal motion amplitudes. The printed L12 stiffness-down arrow is identified as a typo in D2. Assigned membrane frequencies are not generalized to natural rectangle resonances.
